Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Fat-tailed false antechinus (Pseudantechinus macdonnellensis) were obtained through open-flow respirometry on captive individuals maintained under thermoneutral conditions. At a body temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 27.15 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 27.15 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with predictions for small-bodied dasyurid marsupials. This relatively modest metabolic rate likely reflects the species' adaptation to the resource-limited rocky outcrops of central Australia, where energy conservation is prioritized throughout much of the annual cycle. The thermal conditions of these measurements are consistent with the typical active-phase body temperature documented in related Pseudantechinus species, and the data were collected from post-absorptive animals during their nocturnal activity period to ensure basal conditions. Long-term captive studies suggest that variation in ambient temperature influences the resting metabolism, but the standardized 34.2 °C regime used here provides a reliable baseline for interspecific comparisons within the Dasyuridae. Furthermore, the species' small body size and insectivorous diet impose constraints on metabolic scope, with the measured oxygen consumption reflecting the energetic demands of maintaining homeostasis in a thermally challenging environment. These physiological data are essential for understanding the life-history trade-offs that govern survival and reproduction in arid-zone marsupials.

Reproductive output in P. macdonnellensis has been characterized through long-term captive breeding records maintained at the Arid Zone Research Station in Alice Springs. Females produce litters containing an average of six pups [N_R_i = litters containing an average of six pups] and, given the typical annual breeding schedule, this yields a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] under standard captive conditions. The developmental trajectory of these neonates begins with a remarkably small birth mass, with newborn individuals weighing merely 0.0123 grams [Wwb = 0.0123 grams]. This minimal neonatal size is typical among dasyurid marsupials, which rely on a brief gestation period followed by extended lactation within the maternal pouch. The reproductive strategy appears attuned to the seasonal availability of invertebrate prey in the Central Ranges, with females typically entering oestrus during the late winter months to synchronize lactation with peak resource abundance. Captive breeding records also indicate that litter size can occasionally vary from four to eight pups, but six appears to represent the modal value for this species. The remarkably low birth mass, when compared to the asymptotic adult masses of 43 and 45 grams, underscores the extreme altriciality that characterizes this lineage.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a prolonged developmental period, with individuals first attaining puberty at 350 days since birth [tp = 350 days since birth], an interval that spans nearly an entire year of growth and physiological development under the prevailing thermal regime of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. This relatively late onset of reproductive capability may be linked to the necessity of achieving sufficient body mass before the energetic demands of reproduction can be sustained, a pattern observed in other small dasyurids inhabiting unpredictable environments. Concurrently, the weaning process in P. macdonnellensis occurs considerably earlier, with young achieving nutritional independence from maternal milk at 106 days since birth [tx = 106 days since birth], again measured at the species' characteristic active body temperature at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. The extended interval between weaning and puberty represents a critical juvenile growth phase during which subadults must accumulate somatic reserves while navigating an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall and fluctuating prey abundance. Field observations corroborate that young born early in the season have a longer pre-reproductive period, potentially enhancing their condition at first breeding.

Adult body mass exhibits a modest but consistent sexual dimorphism in the Fat-tailed false antechinus, a pattern typical of many dasyurid species where males tend to attain larger ultimate sizes. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of 43 grams [Wwi = 43 grams], while males, which experience reduced post-reproductive survival due to the well-documented semelparous mating system of closely related antechinus species, attain a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 45 grams [Wwi = 45 grams]. This dimorphism, although subtle, is thought to be driven by intrasexual competition among males during the short, intense breeding season. The recorded asymptotic masses were derived from longitudinal captive studies of individuals provided with ad libitum food, and thus likely represent the upper boundary of condition-dependent body size achievable under optimal dietary conditions in this species. Compared to other members of the genus Pseudantechinus, including the more widespread P. ningbing, P. macdonnellensis exhibits a relatively high adult mass, possibly reflecting adaptation to the cooler, more productive rocky ranges. This sexual size difference, while modest in absolute terms, carries implications for metabolic scaling and reproductive energetics.

Lifespan data indicate a maximum documented longevity of 7 years [am = 7 years] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], which exceeds that of many smaller congeneric species and suggests a relatively slow-paced life history compared to smaller dasyurids with shorter lifespans. Gestation in this species proceeds over a period of 43 days [tg = 43 days], measured at the same standard active body temperature, yielding altricial neonates that complete much of their early development attached to a teat within the maternal pouch at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. The extended gestation relative to some eutherian mammals of similar mass likely reflects the unique demands of marsupial embryogenesis, which prioritizes teat attachment structures over somatic development at parturition. Field observations suggest that this reproductive timing allows neonates to emerge from the pouch during the austral spring, when insect abundance peaks across the MacDonnell Ranges. The combination of a long lifespan, a moderate gestation, and low reproductive output per year aligns with a conservative life-history strategy typical of dasyurid marsupials occupying stable but resource-limited environments.
